newsitem.title: TANZANIA: European Union backs Tanzania coffee reforms.
newsitem.headline: European Union backs Tanzania coffee reforms.

text.p: The European Union says Tanzania's coffee is of world class and that it will continue to back reforms in support of the country's agricultural mainstay, a senior EU diplomat said on Friday.

Annual coffee production had fallen in recent years in Tanzania, but market reforms started in 1994 with EU assistance had shown positive results, Ranieri Sabatucci, First Secretary of a European Commission delegation to Tanzania, told Reuters.
"You can argue that coffee production has gone down in the past two or three years but that doesn't mean it's become less profitable," Sabatucci said.
"Because of liberalisation and privatisation they are making profits on a smaller production. Before they were making losses on a bigger production because of inefficiency caused by state marketing."
Tanzania's output for 1996/97 is expected to be about 41-45,000 tonnes, compared with 53,000 tonnes in 1995/96.
EU funding in support of Tanzania's coffee industry has totalled about 100 million Ecus since 1977.

The main area of EU support is through the Stabex (Stabilisation of Export Revenue) programme, under which farmers receive cash compensation when prices or production fall. The latest payment made on March 31 was $11.5 million Ecus and covered losses incurred in 1992/93.
March Stabex funds of around 20.8 million Ecus also covered credit facilities for inputs, feeder road improvements and seedling production.
Sabatucci said the EU was tendering for a consultancy group to study the coffee sector.

The study, to begin later this year, will include a survey of 600 coffee farmers throughout Tanzania's coffee growing regions. One of the biggest problems for the industry is the large number of smallholders occupying plots averaging half to one hectare, or less than 500 trees.
Tanzania produces about one percent of the coffee on the world market, and 75 percent of output is mild arabica of a quality similar to the highly prized Kenyan and Colombian milds.
According to a report by the EU's coffee management unit, Tanzania could double exports without seeing any downward adjustment in its prices.
Until reforms in 1994, all coffee in Tanzania was marketed through the cooperative unions. However, private buyers are estimated to have purchased up to 80 percent of the 1996/97 crop.
Financial support from the EU had been a key factor in supporting those reforms, Sabatucci said.
